verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this from his Nitishatakam. He is writing about the wicked and the boss nobody can please. He lists every possible move a servant makes. Stay silent and you are dull. Speak up and you are a show-off. Stay close and you are pushy. Keep away and you lack confidence. Be patient and you are weak. Refuse abuse and you are ill-bred. Serving another person is harder than yoga. The verse points out that spite turns every virtue into a fault. You are caught in a loop where every move you make gets turned against you. The verse names that trap so you can see it for what it is.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

reading: You feel unsure whether you are leadership material while your manager gives visible projects to others. In the Ramcharitmanas, Manu tells Vishnu that like a poor man before the wishing tree, he hesitates to ask for what he truly wants because doubt rises in his heart. Today, this speaks to the hesitation you carry: the verse names the shrinking that comes from not knowing the giver's power, without judging the wish itself. You can name what you want anyway, resting in the generosity that is already there.
meaning: Manu speaks to Vishnu after years of austerity. Vishnu offers him any boon he desires. Manu hesitates, comparing himself to a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree yet still holds back, unsure of its power. He admits that doubt rises in his heart. The verse proposes that it is not too late to turn toward what matters, but it takes courage to ask for it. The shrinking you feel when your manager hands projects to others echoes Manu's doubt before the tree. You do not need to prove you are leadership material before you can name what you want.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse_text.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse_text.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.

reading: Your boss points out your mistake in front of everyone, and now you feel you are good for nothing. Arjuna tells Krishna that his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, and his body trembles. When work feels unsafe, your body can show the same honest strain without judging your worth.
meaning: Arjuna speaks these words to Krishna on the battlefield. He sees his own kin standing in the enemy ranks. His body collapses in grief and fear. He tells Krishna that his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles, and his hair stands on end. The verse proposes that even the strongest people can freeze and break down. The teaching begins with that honest collapse rather than with any mask of courage. Your body is showing the same honest strain under your boss's words, and that strain does not measure your worth.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: Since the breakup, weekends have become just you. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet no one else knows this ache, and only his own heart knows the truth of their love. Today, your solitude on these quiet days holds a private grief that words only soften slightly, while the depth of what you miss remains known only to you.
meaning: Ram sends this message to Sita through Hanuman. Sita is captive, threatened by Ravana, and has nearly lost hope. Only the guard Trijata has shown her kindness. Hanuman gives her Ram's ring and tells her the whole story of their separation. Sita replies that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet no one else knows this ache, and only Ram's own heart knows the truth of their love. Since the breakup, your weekends hold a private grief that words only soften slightly, while the depth of what you miss remains known only to you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever sees him everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him, and he is never lost to them. After your divorce, moving to a new city to start fresh left you without a single person you know. This verse speaks of a bond that distance cannot break, where presence remains even when no familiar face is near.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna while teaching him how to settle the mind through meditation. He explains that a person who sees him in everything and sees everything within him shares a bond that distance cannot sever. Neither side is ever lost to the other. After your divorce and move to a new city, you are starting over without anyone you know. This verse speaks of a presence that remains even when no familiar face is near.

verse_text.speaker: the gopis
verse_text.setting: The women of Braj, after Krishna has left, on missing him.
verse_text.line: "Since he left, it has been monsoon in our eyes."
verse_text.translation: Night and day our eyes keep raining. Ever since Shyam went away, it is always the rainy season for us.

reading: Since your closest friend moved abroad, your life feels bare in a way you did not expect. The gopis say that since Shyam left, it has been monsoon in their eyes, night and day raining without stop. Your missing him can feel like weather that simply will not lift, and naming that emptiness plainly is part of the love you still hold.
meaning: The women of Braj speak these words after Krishna has gone away. They tell a friend that night and day their eyes keep raining. Ever since Shyam left, it has been the rainy season for them. The verse says that tears for someone you miss are allowed. Your life feels bare now that your closest friend is abroad. The gopis show that missing someone can feel like weather that simply will not lift, and naming that emptiness plainly is part of the love you still hold.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You have been firefighting so long that nothing remains in the tank. The Yoga Vasishtha has King Bali say that day follows night, and the same chain of tasks repeats again and again, which feels like a mockery to a thinking person. This sense of being stuck in the same loop speaks to that weariness today. Bali keeps sitting by his window rather than walking away, simply noticing the repetition.
meaning: King Bali, who has ruled the three worlds for ages, sits by his window and looks out at his life. He sees that day follows night, and the same chain of tasks repeats again and again. He tells himself that to a thinking person this loop feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the work is not to do more of it but to master the mind that runs it. You have been firefighting so long that nothing remains in the tank. The same loop of demands has worn you down, and that weariness is real.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and do not last. Your work pressure and the fatigue that keeps you in bed on weekends are contacts that touch you and then move on. You can bear this tiredness patiently, noticing that it too has a beginning and an end, without letting it sweep you away.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while the grieving warrior stands on the battlefield. He tells him that contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These experiences come and go and do not last. The teaching is that what you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You are running your own thing, and tonight your mind is spinning about whether the launch will work. Krishna hears Arjuna say that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. That same restlessness can be here with you now, in the dark, without forcing it to stop.
meaning: Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and that it is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees with this description and points out that practice and letting go can train the mind over time. Your mind tonight is doing exactly what Arjuna described, and it does not need to be fixed before morning.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

reading: You feel your colleagues' MBA puts them ahead of your experience, and a sense of smallness rises when you compare yourself to them. In the Ramcharitmanas, Manu speaks of finding the wishing tree yet hesitating to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt fills his heart. That same hesitation can sit with you at work today: the verse names the doubt without judging your worth, and simply points to the tree standing ready, its power still there for you to reach toward.
meaning: Manu speaks to Vishnu after years of austerity in the forest. Vishnu offers him any boon he desires. Manu feels like a poor man who has found the wish-fulfilling tree yet still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its true power. He admits that doubt rises in his heart. The verse proposes that hesitation can block what is already within reach, and that it takes courage to name what matters. Your years of experience are the tree standing before you, yet the doubt that your colleagues hold more pulls your hand back before you ask for what you deserve.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You lose your temper with your child over homework each evening and then hate yourself. The Yoga Vasishtha speaks of a mind caught on endless waves of tasks, forever reckoning what is done, doing, and still to do, so that the bird of the mind faints in its net. In your evenings, that same loop of duties can tighten until a snap escapes, and the verse simply names how the mind never rests when swept along by such waves.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to Vilasa, his childhood friend, after they meet again as old men. Vilasa asks if Bhasa has found any peace after years of hard austerities apart. Bhasa answers that there is no wellness while the mind keeps spinning through endless tasks and worries. He describes a mind carried on great waves of duties, forever reckoning what is done, what is doing, and what must still be done, so that the bird of the mind faints in its net and finds no rest. Your evenings with homework have become one of those endless waves, and the snap that follows is the mind fainting under the weight of its own lists.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You described a weekly clash where a slammed door leads to yelling and both of you feel awful. Bhasa says the mind is carried along on endless waves of tasks, fainting in a net of reckonings: 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do.' In the middle of that loop today, the verse simply names the spinning, without judging the noise. You might notice the bird of the mind, tangled in the list of done, doing, and still to do, and let that image sit beside the slammed door.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to Vilasa, his childhood friend, when the two old men meet again after years of lonely austerity. Vilasa has admitted he never found peace. Bhasa answers that the mind is carried on endless waves of tasks. It never rests. It dances with worry. The bird of the mind faints, tangled in a net of reckonings that say this I have done, this I am doing, and this I must do. The weekly clash with your teenager is one wave in that endless list. The verse names the spinning mind that keeps tally of done, doing, and still to do, without saying the door slam is your fault or your cure.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You are furious at your lead for dumping work on you, and after snapping in standup you feel like the problem. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born; from attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger. Your flare-up in the meeting is the final link in a chain that began earlier, in the moments you kept turning the unfair load over in your mind. The work still sits on your plate, and the standup is over.
meaning: Krishna answers Arjuna's question about the steady person. He explains that when someone dwells on objects, attachment is born. From that attachment comes desire, and from desire comes anger. Your flare-up in standup is the final link in a chain that began earlier, when you kept turning the unfair load over in your mind.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You are waiting on emergency leave while your dad is in hospice in Delhi. Krishna, far from home, tells his mother that since he left, no one has called him by his pet name, and he has missed his morning breakfast and evening warm milk. In your distance right now, the ache may be for those small, ordinary signs of home rather than grand gestures. You might let yourself notice what you are actually missing as you wait.
meaning: Krishna is in Mathura, far from his home. He sends a message to his mother Yashoda. He tells her that since the day he left, no one has called him by his pet name Kanhaiya. He also says he has not eaten morning breakfast or had warm milk in the evening. The verse says that missing home shows itself through these small, daily signs of care. Your distance right now may carry the ache of those small, ordinary signs of home rather than grand gestures. You might let yourself notice what you are actually missing as you wait.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
verse_text.translation: It is never born and never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

reading: Watching your mother slowly leave feels unbearable. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. You do not have to accept this today, but you can let it sit quietly beside the grief, holding the truth that what she most deeply is was never ended by her body's fading.
meaning: Krishna speaks these words to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is overcome with grief at the thought of fighting his own kin. Krishna tells him that the true self inside every person was never born and will never die. It remains eternal and unchanged even when the body is destroyed. The verse points to the deathless core that outlasts all physical loss. Your mother's body is fading, yet the verse speaks of a core that no illness can end. It does not ask you to feel less pain today.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You missed your mother's surgery because leave was denied, and her saying it is fine has not quieted the thought. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their will, as if pushed by force. The verse names this inner push as real, not proof that you are bad, and it meets the weight of your mind today in that single missed day.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even when they do not want to, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this anger clouds a person's wisdom like smoke over fire. He tells Arjuna to see this force clearly so he can master it. The missed day was not a sign that you are bad. It was the result of a desire you could not meet, and that unmet want is now sitting heavy in your mind.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: Arjuna asks this, and many of us ask it too: what pushes a person to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? If you're carrying something you did, you've probably asked it at night. The Gita treats the question as worth a full answer.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong against their own will, as if pushed by some outside force. Krishna answers that desire which has not been met turns into anger. This anger clouds a person's wisdom and becomes the hidden enemy that drives them to act against what they know is right. The anger you felt toward your father came from a desire that was blocked, and now the guilt is what remains visible to you.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: Arjuna asks this, and many of us ask it too: what pushes a person to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? If you're carrying something you did, you've probably asked it at night. The Gita treats the question as worth a full answer.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong against their own will, as if pushed by some outside force. Krishna answers that it is desire which has not been met. When that desire is blocked, it turns into anger. This anger clouds a person's wisdom and judgment like smoke covering a fire. The verse proposes that you see this chain clearly so you can master it rather than be ruled by it. You asked the Gita a question that fits your own night right now. It names the force you felt when you yelled at your grandmother.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You lost the partnership after saying unforgivable things in a rage, and now the guilt stays. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, which blocked turns into anger. The verse points to the moment before the snap, where the mind keeps turning something over until it hardens into wanting. You might notice where your thoughts have been dwelling today, and what that quiet brooding has been building toward.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna what a person of steady mind looks like in speech and action. Krishna answers that such a person rests within and is not shaken by sorrow. He then traces how the mind ruins itself. When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and from desire, when it is blocked, anger arises. Your anger arrived after weeks of turning the same grievances over in your mind, and now the guilt remains because the dwelling did not stop before the snap.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Anger clouds judgement, clouded judgement loses memory, lost memory wrecks reason, and then you fall.
verse_text.translation: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, confusion of memory; from confusion of memory, the ruin of understanding; and with understanding ruined, a person is lost.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that from anger comes delusion, then confusion of memory, then the ruin of understanding, and finally you fall. The part of you that knew better had already left the room before the words reached your partner. Today, you can notice the moment that clarity slips, and choose silence until the surge passes.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: It's desire, which turns into anger when blocked. Never satisfied, it is the real enemy here.
verse_text.translation: The Blessed Lord said: It is desire, it is anger, born of the quality of passion; all-devouring and greatly harmful. Know this to be the enemy here.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that desire, which turns into anger when blocked, is the real enemy here. It is born of restless passion and can never be satisfied. You felt the anger come fast and the guilt stay; tracing that flash back to a blocked want gives you ground to stand on today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Unshaken in sorrow, not craving in joy, free of clinging, fear and anger: that is a steady mind.
verse_text.translation: One whose mind is not shaken by sorrow, who has no craving for pleasures, and who is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady mind.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that a steady mind is unshaken by sorrow, without craving in joy, and free from attachment, fear and anger. This describes a sage whose feelings still arise, yet sorrow, fear or anger do not drive the response. After the earlier verses on how anger clouds judgment, this offers you ground: the mind can hold the fast guilt without being ruled by the same anger that snapped at your partner.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Whoever can ride out the surge of desire and anger, here and now, is steady and happy.
verse_text.translation: One who is able, here in this life, before leaving the body, to withstand the surge born of desire and anger, is disciplined; he is a happy person.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever can withstand the surge of desire and anger right here, in this life, is steady and happy. You could place a hand on your desk the next time heat rises, and simply wait for the wave to pass before you speak. The guilt stays, yet the surge itself will fall.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on three kinds of food, effort, speech and giving.
verse_text.line: Speak words that don't wound, that are true, kind and helpful. That is discipline of speech.
verse_text.translation: Speech that causes no distress, that is truthful, pleasant and beneficial, and the regular study of sacred texts: this is called austerity of speech.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that disciplined speech means words that do not wound, that are true, kind and helpful. After the surge of anger passes, you could test your next words against these four marks before letting them out. This keeps the truth of your point without adding cruelty on top of the damage already done.

story.title: Vishvamitra's vow
story.summary: Vishvamitra had given up a kingdom to become a sage, and had already started his effort over more than once. Then, tested again, he lost his temper and cursed the apsara Rambha, and with that curse the power of his long austerity was spent. This time he made a vow: he would not give way to anger, or even speak. He kept a long silence. Obstacles came again and shook him, but anger couldn't get in. In the end he reached his goal, and Vasishtha, the rival he had once fought, embraced him as a friend.
story.lesson: Relapses happen. A clear vow and steady practice can loosen anger's grip.

days.reading: Vishvamitra vowed not to yield to anger or even speak, and after a long silence he held firm through fresh obstacles until he reached his goal, with his old rival becoming a friend. The story shows that a clear vow and steady practice can loosen anger's grip, even after a relapse like the one you described. You can mark a similar pause today—perhaps choosing silence over speech—and let that steadiness carry you forward.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You dropped out and nothing seems worth the effort anymore. Young Rama asks, What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for? When everything you once chased feels empty, that question is not a dead end. It is the doorway to finding what actually matters for you.
meaning: Young Rama has just come back from his travels and sits in his father's court. The sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask him why he looks so empty. Rama answers with a string of questions. He asks what kingship means to him and what pleasures are. He asks who he is and what all this is for. He says if it is unreal, let it be unreal. He asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. The verse proposes that naming honestly what feels empty is the first step. When the path you were on has vanished and effort feels pointless, that emptiness is not a failure. It is the honest starting point for finding what might matter next.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You worked hard yet nothing came of it, and now nothing feels like it matters. Young Rama asks, What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for? If it is unreal, let it be unreal. This questioning of everything you chased can be the start of a real inquiry into who you are, opening a space to explore what might matter beyond the effort itself.
meaning: Young Rama returns to his father's court after his travels. He speaks to the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha. He tells them that nothing interests him anymore. He asks what kingship and pleasure mean to him. He asks who he is and what all this is for. He says if it is unreal, let it be unreal. He wants to know whose it is and what anyone has gained. The verse proposes that naming honestly what feels empty is the first step. Rama's words are a question, not the answer. You poured your effort into work and still nothing came of it. Now the very idea of reward feels hollow. Rama names that emptiness without rushing to fix it.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You have spent 15 years in 12-hour days building this business, and now the routine leaves you feeling empty and tired. Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and says that day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over, mocks a thinking person. That same loop of repetition can speak to you today, naming the exhaustion behind your autopilot, without asking you to walk away from what you have built.
meaning: Bali, a demon king who has ruled the three worlds for ages, sits by his window and looks out at his endless days. He speaks to himself about the cycle of day and night and the same tasks rising and falling like waves. He says that to a thinking person this repetition feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it. After fifteen years of long days you built this business and now the routine leaves you empty and tired. The verse names that loop without asking you to walk away from what you have built.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.
verse_text.line: The mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy.
verse_text.translation: The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy.

reading: You end up scrolling until 1am instead of studying after work. Rama tells the sages that the mind swoops onto a task like a bird onto meat, then drops it like a bored child's toy. This pattern is simply how an untrained mind behaves, not a mark against you. Tonight, when the urge to pick up your phone arises, notice the swoop and set a single page of your book open on the desk.
meaning: Rama speaks to the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha after they ask why he has grown so withdrawn. He is describing what he sees in himself. The mind swoops onto a task like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy. He is naming the restless habit of the untrained mind, which grabs at whatever attracts it and then abandons even worthwhile work almost at once. You are caught in the same swoop between work and the screen, and naming it is the first honest step.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You have a firm resolve to prepare for GATE, yet starting each day consumes half your time. Savitri tells her father-in-law that she began this hard vow with determination, and that same determination will carry it to the end. Let that steady resolve be what pulls you through the morning hours today, until the work itself is done.
meaning: Savitri speaks to her blind father-in-law Dyumatsena. She knows her husband Satyavan will die in three days. She has begun a severe three night vow without food. Dyumatsena worries at its harshness. Savitri tells him not to grieve. She says she started the vow with determination. That same determination will carry it to the end. Your resolve for GATE is solid. The same drive that made you choose this path can carry you through the morning fog each day.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: Your business had its best year ever, and you feel thankful while wanting to keep your feet on the ground. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one the world follows. Because people look to you, your grounded way of carrying this success becomes the quiet example others may follow.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has been wondering why anyone should act when wisdom is already within. Krishna answers that people do not follow words. They copy what a respected person actually does. The standard that person sets becomes the one the world follows. Even those who have no personal need to gain anything keep working, because others watch their conduct and take it as their guide. Your business reached its best year, and you want to stay steady inside that success. The verse points to the weight of being watched, and how your grounded conduct quietly shapes what others around you take as normal.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel that everything is good, with peace and gratitude in your heart. The poet marvels at freedom to wander, food eaten without humiliation, noble company, learning that brings calm, and a mind that stirs only gently. In this quiet season of life, you can rest in the wonder of these simple dignities you already hold, letting your gratitude settle into the morning itself.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his Worship of Shiva. He is reflecting on the life of a quiet seeker by the Ganga. He lists freedom to move, food taken with dignity, good company, study that brings calm, and a gentle mind. He marvels at these simple goods and wonders what great effort or austerity could have ripened into such a life. He does not claim to have earned them. He simply stands in wonder at their presence. In this quiet season you already hold these simple dignities. You can rest in the wonder of them without trying to explain where they came from.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You feel drawn to Krishna in a way you did not expect. Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those seeking wealth, and the wise. Your unexpected pull toward the divine counts as one of these welcome doors, and it can simply rest there with you today as you raise your kids.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded and the wrongdoers do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. He says the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise all worship him. He means that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Your unexpected pull toward Krishna is one of these four welcome doors, and it does not need a reason beyond itself.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You feel peaceful and want to go deeper, perhaps toward God. Krishna says the one who is happy within, at ease within, and lit from within finds lasting freedom. As your meditation and chanting settle, you might notice a gladness that does not wait for anything outside to change, rooted in the quiet you are already cultivating.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna on the battlefield. He is describing the sage who has seen clearly. The verse says that when a person's happiness, delight and light all come from inside, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman. It proposes that pleasures which begin and end cannot hold your happiness. The joy must be found within. You have found a calm through meditation and chanting, and now you want to go deeper toward God. This verse points to the gladness that already lives inside that quiet practice.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You long for the joy found in singing bhajans to remain present in every moment. Krishna tells Arjuna that people turn to the divine in distress, curiosity, need, or wisdom, and he calls all four kinds good. This means the delight you feel while singing is already a worthy way to meet what you love, and you can let that same sweetness stay with you today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after noting that wrongdoers and the deluded do not turn to him. He names four kinds of people who do worship him. These are the distressed, the curious, those in need, and the wise. He calls all four good. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. It does not demand a pure motive or a single reason. The joy you find in singing bhajans is already a worthy way to meet what you love. That sweetness can stay with you today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: Karmaṇy evādhikāras te: your right is to the action. Fear of failure is a fear about the fruit, which was never given to you to control. Krishna also closes the escape route: don't let this make you stop acting. Care, prepare and aim well, then put the outcome down.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on a battlefield before a great war. Arjuna is afraid to fight. Krishna tells him to do his duty fully. The outcome belongs to forces beyond Arjuna. Krishna says do not stop acting just because the result is uncertain. Your launch is your work. The money that follows belongs to a future you cannot hold right now. Do the work fully and set the outcome down.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You are carrying extra work after half the team was cut, waiting to see if you are next. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and do not last; we must bear them. This restlessness can meet the fact that the heavier load, too, is a passing contact, not a permanent state, and it will move on.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving the coming war and the loss of his kin. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These experiences come and go. They do not last. Arjuna must bear them patiently. Your restlessness sits inside a heavier load that is still shifting, not a fixed fate.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: Ram says the deepest sorrow was not the exile itself, but that the king did not face him and tell him directly. When harsh words from your husband’s family keep burning you day after day, the verse names that the sting often lies in how the blow reached you, not merely what it was. You can hold that precise hurt today: the pain of being pushed away without a clear, honest facing of you.
meaning: Rama speaks these words to Kaikeyi after he has calmly agreed to fourteen years in the forest. His father has ordered his exile and Bharata's coronation. Rama accepts the decree without anger. Yet one thing still burns him. He says only his father did not tell him this himself. The verse proposes that a person can bear bad news, but the wound often lies in who delivered it and how. Your husband accepted the pressure from his family and left. The verse shows that the exile itself can be accepted, yet the deeper burn is that no one faced you directly to say what was happening.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
verse_text.translation: It is never born and never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

reading: You carry the hurt of missing your dad’s cremation. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is. Let that truth sit quietly beside your grief, not as a command, but as a companion to the ache of not being there.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is shaken by the thought of killing his own kin. Krishna tells him that the self was never born and will never die. It existed before and will exist after. When the body is slain it is not slain. The self simply outlasts the body. Your father's body has passed, and you were not there to stand by the fire. The verse speaks of what outlasts the body, not of the moment you missed.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: As we drop worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self leaves a worn body for a new one.
verse_text.translation: Just as a person casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that as we cast off worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self leaves a worn body for a new one. This image gives you ground to stand on today, letting the loss be as big as it is without forcing the finality of it. You can rest in the picture of setting aside something worn, while the grief you carry remains real.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Childhood, youth, old age: the body keeps changing. The wise aren't thrown by the next change.
verse_text.translation: Just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it passes on to another body. The steady person is not bewildered by this.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the embodied self passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, and then moves on to another body, so the steady person is not bewildered by this change. You already watched your dad change across his life, and now the body has shifted once more. This verse gives you ground to stand on: the self stays the same through every stage, including this last one.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: No weapon cuts it, no fire burns it, no water wets it, no wind dries it.
verse_text.translation: Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, and wind does not dry it.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that no weapon cuts the self, no fire burns it, no water wets it, and no wind dries it. Whatever reached your father’s body in India did not reach who he was. You stand on the ground that his essence remained beyond the reach of the flames and the distance you could not cross.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha on the fourth gatekeeper: good company (satsanga).
verse_text.line: Even at your lowest and most helpless, don't let go of good company.
verse_text.translation: Even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little.

days.reading: Vasishtha tells Rama that even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little. After walking through the body’s changes and the self’s endurance, this points you to keep one thread to someone steady—a wise friend, a mentor, or a trusted circle—even for a few minutes. Let that small contact be your ground today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse_text.line: A leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water: whatever is offered with love, I accept.
verse_text.translation: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, that offering of love from the pure-hearted I accept.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that he accepts a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or a little water when offered with love. You could place a flower or a small glass of water somewhere today, letting your love for your dad have a simple place to rest. The gesture itself is enough.

story.title: Bharata returns to Ayodhya
story.summary: Bharata was far away at his grandfather's home when his father, King Dasharatha, died. Messengers called him back without telling him why. He rode into an Ayodhya that had gone quiet, went looking for his father, and learned he was gone. He fell to the ground and wept. When he could stand again, the family priest Vasishtha gently told him it was time to perform the last rites, and he did them, grieving as he went.
story.lesson: Missing the goodbye is its own grief. Let yourself feel it, then do what love asks next.

days.reading: In the Ramayana, Bharata returns to Ayodhya to find his father Dasharatha dead and learns the last rites are already done. He falls to the ground and weeps, then performs what love asks next while grieving. You carry the ache of reaching India too late for the cremation; let that missing the goodbye be its own grief, then do what love asks next.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You are stretched across office deadlines, your son's exam prep, and a toddler. The Yoga Vasishtha says the mind, caught in 'done this, doing this, must do that,' faints in a net of reckonings and never gets a moment's rest. Today, that endless wave of tasks may be exactly what is keeping you awake. You might notice one small gap between one task and the next, and let the depths simply pause there.
meaning: Two old friends meet again after many years apart. Bhasa admits to Vilasa that he never found peace. He says the mind is carried along on endless waves of tasks. It never gets a moment's rest because it keeps counting what is done, what is happening, and what still must be done. The mind faints in that net of reckonings. You are carrying office deadlines, your son's exam prep, and a toddler all at once. The verse names the exact loop that is wearing you down.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: With work ramping up, daycare calling about a fever, and your partner away, the pressure feels relentless right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact with the world brings heat and cold, pleasure and pain, and these pass without lasting. You can notice that this strain, like a fever, has its own beginning and end, and sit with it as it moves through your day.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield of after Arjuna has laid down his weapons in grief. He tells him that the senses meeting their objects produce cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These arrive and depart like shifts in the air. They do not stay. So Arjuna must bear them with patience. Your present pressure has a beginning and an end, even when it feels endless. You can sit with it without letting it swallow your whole day.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You are starting your dream job on Monday, feeling excited and terrified you will mess it up. Lakshmana tells Ram that there is no strength greater than enthusiasm, and for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. Your hope already carries that energy; let it meet the work itself, one step at a time, beginning Monday.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Rama is overwhelmed by longing for Sita. Every bird and mated deer reminds him of her and his grief deepens. Lakshmana answers this long lament by praising resolute energy. He tells Rama that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. With that energy alone, little in the world remains unattainable. Your excitement for Monday already holds the force Lakshmana names. The terror that you might falter does not cancel it out. Let that energy meet the work itself, one step at a time.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You have been going back and forth on leaving your job for months, and it occupies your thoughts day and night. Arjuna tells Krishna that his nature is stricken by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right, and he asks plainly to be taught what is best. In the same spirit, you can set down the argument you have been running and simply present the question of what to do next to a clearer source, without forcing an answer tonight.
meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield. He has just collapsed in tears. He refuses to fight his revered elders. Krishna tells him to shake off his faint heartedness. Arjuna replies that his nature is stricken by weakness. His mind is confused about what is right. He asks Krishna to tell him for certain what is best. He says he is Krishna's student and has come to be taught. You too have reached a point where your own judgement feels blocked by the weight of the choice.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You described rushing between your full-time job, your two young children, and your husband's night shifts, with tiredness that holidays do not fix. The Yoga Vasishtha has Bhasa tell Vilasa that a mind caught on waves of 'done this, doing this, must do that' never rests, its depths dancing with worry. Today, your to-do lists may feel like that endless net, and the verse simply names that the mind faints under such reckoning. Notice one small task today where you can pause the list, even for a breath.
meaning: Two old friends meet again after many years apart. Bhasa tells Vilasa that no one finds peace while the mind keeps spinning through tasks. He says the mind is carried on great waves of duties, its depths dancing with worry. It repeats done this, doing this, must do that. Caught in that net of reckonings, the bird of the mind faints. Your tiredness that holidays cannot fix is the mind caught in that same endless reckoning, not a lack of rest.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: With your presentation tomorrow, your mind is racing and hard to steady. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy and as hard to hold as the wind. That same restlessness can sit with you right now, without pushing it away or forcing it quiet.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes a steady person who feels all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such calm cannot last. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He thinks it is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse proposes that the mind is difficult to steady, yet practice and letting go can train it over time. Your mind is racing before the presentation. Arjuna names that same restlessness honestly, and it is the starting point for practice, not proof that you cannot do this.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You are caught between bringing your widowed dad to Australia and moving back to be with him, and both paths cost someone something. Arjuna tells Krishna that his nature is stricken by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right, and he asks plainly to be taught. In the same way, you can lay this torn choice before what you trust most and ask for clarity, without forcing the answer yourself right now.
meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield and speaks to Krishna. He has just refused to fight his own teachers and granduncle. His body shakes with grief and his mind cannot tell which choice is worse. He admits that his own strength has failed him. He asks Krishna to teach him plainly what is best. The verse proposes that clarity begins when a person admits they do not know and asks for guidance as a student. You are facing a choice where both paths take something from someone you love, and your own mind has run out of answers.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You are caught between bringing your mother to you or going to Patna, and you do not know which path is right. Arjuna tells Krishna that his mind is confused about what is right, and he asks plainly to be taught what is best. Today, your honesty about not knowing can be the place where clarity begins, as you sit with this one concrete step: reaching out to her today to share what is in your heart.
meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield. He has dropped his bow. He tells Krishna that his mind is clouded and he cannot see what is right. He asks Krishna to teach him plainly what is best. He says he is ready to learn as a student.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You find it hard to congratulate your batchmate after being passed over yourself. Bhartrihari speaks to his own hope, saying he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart, asking how much longer hope will make him dance. Today, you might recognise that same hollow feeling when you try to smile for someone else's gain. You can set down the performance, even just for today, and let your own disappointment sit quietly beside you.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to his own hope from the Censure of Craving. He tells how he endured taunts from wicked people while trying to please them. He held back his tears and laughed with an empty heart. He even folded his hands before those whose minds were numbed by money. He asks hope how much longer it will make him dance in this futile way. You are facing a moment where someone else's gain sits right across from your own stall, and the gap feels raw.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You keep buying things and upgrading, yet nothing fills the space. Young Rama asks what kingship or pleasure mean to him, and who he is beneath it all. This emptiness you feel can be the start of asking what truly matters, rather than a dead end. Let that question sit with you as you look at the next thing on your list.
meaning: Young Rama returns from his travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra asks why he looks so low. Rama answers that he has seen how wealth hardens people, how life slips away, and how the mind never fills. He asks what kingship or pleasure mean to him, who he really is, and what anyone gains from all this. The verse proposes that naming this emptiness honestly is the first step toward real inquiry. Your cycle of upgrades and new purchases mirrors Rama's court, where every gain felt hollow. This emptiness is not a flaw in you. It is the opening of a question about what you are actually chasing.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You have put down your bow after applying to many jobs since your company shut down, and your mind feels overwhelmed by grief. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief. verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You come home to an empty apartment and wonder what any of it is for. Young Rama asks the same: what is a kingdom, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for? His question is treated as the healthy start of inquiry, not a dead end. Today, that same question can sit with you in the silence, pointing toward who you are beyond the routine.
meaning: Young Rama has just returned from his travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask him why he looks so low. Rama answers that he has seen how wealth hardens people and how life slips away. He asks what a kingdom or pleasure means to him. He asks who he really is and what all this is for. He says if it is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. Your empty apartment and the loop of eat and sleep carry the same weight Rama names. The text sees this not as a failure but as the first honest step toward a real question.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You trained your nephew, yet he took your biggest clients and opened his own shop. Bhartrihari tells the reader that keeping quiet makes you dull, while speaking up brands you a show-off; any behaviour can be read as a fault when you serve someone powerful. Today, this double bind speaks to the unfairness you face after giving your knowledge away, showing that the trap lies in the position itself, not in you. Notice how your own trained hand now works across the street, and let that reality sit with you.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this to the reader from his section on wicked people. He is describing the impossible position of anyone who serves a master. No matter what the servant does, the master twists it into a fault. If the servant stays quiet, the master calls them dull. If they speak well, the master calls them a show-off. If they stay close, they are pushy. If they keep away, they lack confidence. If they are patient, they are weak. If they refuse to endure, they are ill bred. You gave your knowledge to someone you trusted, and now that same hand works across the street with your biggest clients. The verse shows that the trap is in the position, not in your worth or your teaching.

verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: When your partner breaks an agreement and your temper spikes, then you lie awake replaying how loud you got, you are facing a mind that refuses to settle. verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You feel stuck while others move ahead. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna, the greatest archer, put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. This verse names the moment of laying everything down when you cannot go on. It points to a place where you can set down what you are carrying alone in your spare room.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra. He reports the moment Arjuna stands on the battlefield and gives up. Arjuna lowers his bow and arrows. He sits down in his chariot. His mind is overwhelmed by grief. The verse states that even the strongest person can freeze when the weight becomes too much. You are watching peers move ahead while you carry the work alone in your spare room. This verse names the exact moment of laying everything down when you cannot go on.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You feel the sting of seeing your juniors from your first job reach CXO roles. The poet Bhartrihari cries out to his own hope, saying he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart, asking how much longer hope will make him dance. Today, this verse names the pattern of enduring humiliation for a gain that may never arrive, without judging your pain. You might notice where you are still performing approval, and let that awareness sit with the actual updates you see.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks to his own hope from a place of weariness. He tells it that he endured the taunts of wicked people while trying to please them. He held back his tears and laughed with an empty heart. He even folded his hands before those whose minds were numbed by money. He asks hope how much longer it will make him dance in this way. Your juniors have reached the top while you remain where you are. The verse names the cost of waiting for recognition that may never come, without asking you to dismiss your hurt.

It begins the teaching from a place of breakdown, not strength.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

reading: You notice the other mums at school pickup and feel behind. Krishna tells Arjuna that doing your own work, even imperfectly, is better than performing another's duty perfectly. Your choice to step back from a career fits your own path, and walking it honestly carries no wrong.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna on the battlefield of after listing duties tied to different stations in life. Arjuna stands in doubt about his role as a warrior. Krishna tells him that one reaches perfection by doing the work born of one's own nature as an offering. He adds that one's own path, even if walked with flaws, is better than another's done perfectly. Acting in line with one's own nature brings no fault. You stepped back from a career to raise your children. That choice fits your own path, and walking it honestly carries no wrong even when it looks messier than the lives around you.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You carry the ache of being the other one at every family dinner. Ram says only one sorrow burns his heart: that the king did not tell him himself about Bharata's coronation. The deepest hurt can be that the person you love did not face you directly. That unnamed distance at the table names what you feel today.
meaning: In the Ayodhya Kanda of the Valmiki Ramayana, Rama speaks to Kaikeyi after he has agreed to fourteen years of exile. He has accepted the loss of his kingdom without anger. Yet one sorrow still burns him. He tells Kaikeyi that the news itself did not wound him most. What hurt was that his father, the king, did not come to him and tell him directly about Bharata's coronation. The verse proposes that a person can accept a hard fate. You carry the ache of being the other one at every family dinner. The verse names that the wound is not the outcome alone, but the way it reaches you through others instead of the one you love.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has lain on the shore for three days asking the ocean for a way across. No answer comes.
verse_text.line: Calm, patience, honesty and kind words: people who don't value them will read them as weakness.
verse_text.translation: See the ocean's arrogance: he does not even show himself. Calm, forbearance, straightforwardness and gentle speech, these virtues of the good, are taken by the unworthy as signs of weakness.

days.reading: Ram tells Lakshman that the ocean’s silence makes his calm, patience, honesty and kind words look like weakness to the unworthy. Your hurt can sit beside this: the verse sees the misreading coming from the other person’s lack, not from any fault in your gentleness. At your next family dinner, you might simply notice who reads your quiet as small, while the text names their arrogance, not your worth.

verse_text.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse_text.speaker: Prahlada (quoted by Draupadi)
verse_text.setting: Draupadi quotes old Prahlada answering his grandson: is forgiveness better, or force?
verse_text.line: Force isn't always right, and forgiveness isn't always right. Wisdom is knowing which the moment needs.
verse_text.translation: Force is not always best, and forgiveness is not always best. Know this for certain, my child: both have their place.

days.reading: Draupadi quotes Prahlada telling Bali that force is not always best, and forgiveness is not always best either; wisdom is knowing which the moment needs. You do not have to choose between swallowing hurt and striking back right now. Standing on this, you can simply notice what this moment actually calls for, without rushing either way.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Uttanka, furious that the war happened, threatens to curse Krishna for not stopping it.
verse_text.line: I tried hard to make peace. When people refuse to be reconciled, you can't force it.
verse_text.translation: I made every effort earlier to bring the Kauravas to peace. But they could not be brought to agree, however I tried.

days.reading: Krishna tells the sage Uttanka that he tried hard to bring the Kauravas to peace, yet they refused to agree no matter how he pleaded. You do not have to carry the weight of a rift that stays closed despite your own honest effort. Notice where you stand today, and let that be enough ground beneath you.

verse_text.speaker: Seer
verse_text.setting: The creation story: last of all, dharma is made.
verse_text.line: Nothing is higher than what is right. With it the weak can face the strong. What is right is truth.
verse_text.translation: Still he did not flourish. So he created a higher form, dharma. Dharma is the power over power; nothing is higher than dharma. Through dharma even a weak man can stand up to a strong one, as with the help of a king. That dharma is truth. So people say of one who speaks truth, 'He speaks dharma,' and of one who speaks dharma, 'He speaks truth.' Both are the same.

days.reading: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says Brahman created dharma last, and nothing is higher than what is right. Through it, the weak can face the strong, and what is right is truth. You could anchor yourself in what is fair today, letting that steadiness be your standing place against the comparison at family dinners.

verse_text.setting: Ram is lost and grieving; Kabandha tells him to seek Sugriva, who has also lost his wife and home.
verse_text.line: Find a friend who knows your kind of trouble. You won't get through this alone.

days.reading: Kabandha tells Ram, who is lost and grieving, to seek Sugriva, who has also lost his wife and home: find a friend who knows your kind of trouble, because you won't get through this alone. story.title: Hanuman finds a friend in Lanka
story.summary: Searching Lanka, Hanuman is surprised to find a house with Ram's name on it. Its owner, Vibhishan, Ravana's brother, says he lives in Lanka like a tongue among teeth. Hanuman tells him even a restless monkey like himself was given Ram's love.
story.lesson: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.

days.reading: Vibhishan tells Hanuman he lives inside Lanka like a tongue among teeth, surrounded by people whose values he does not share, with no one to speak to. Hanuman, who also feels least, does not lecture him but meets him as one who trusts in Ram's grace. In your hurt, this scene speaks to the loneliness of being the other one at family dinners, and shows that one true conversation with someone who knows your kind of trouble can bring rest beyond words.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
