verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You are carrying the weight of being torn down in front of everyone at work. Bhartrihari cries out to hope, saying he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart, asking how much longer this dance will continue. Today, you might notice the cost of keeping up appearances when your report was dismissed as bakwas before all. You do not have to keep dancing to a hope that asks you to empty your own heart.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks to his own hope after confessing that he dug for treasure and flattered kings for gain. He tells hope that he swallowed insults from wicked people, held back his tears, laughed with an empty heart, and folded his hands before those numbed by money. He asks how much longer hope will make him dance in this futile way. You are swallowing humiliation at work because a small hope keeps you there. The verse names that price without blaming you for staying.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that it is better to walk one's own path imperfectly than to perform another's duty perfectly. You have been acting head for two years, and now a younger outsider has been chosen for the permanent role. This verse invites you to see the value in the work you have already done from your own standing, rather than measuring it against someone else's arrival.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield of after Arjuna has laid down his bow in despair. Krishna has just explained that perfection comes through worship offered via one's own work. He now tells Arjuna that his own duty, even if walked imperfectly, is better than another's duty performed perfectly. Doing work that fits one's own nature brings no fault, because every undertaking carries some flaw.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You feel angry because your ideas only get heard when a guy repeats them in the meeting. Bhartrihari says that when you serve someone powerful, keeping quiet makes you dull and speaking up makes you a show-off; any behaviour can be read as a fault. This speaks to you today as a description of the bind you are in, not a flaw in you. You might anchor in your own standard of contribution, and notice one moment in the next meeting when your original words stand on their own.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this from a section on wicked people. He addresses anyone who serves a master. At court, a servant faces a trap. Stay silent and you are called dull. Speak well and you are called a babbler. Stay close and you are pushy. Keep away and you lack confidence. Be patient and you are weak. Refuse to endure and you are ill bred. The duty of serving another is a deep bind. Even those who practice yoga cannot easily escape it. Your anger makes sense. A man at work repeats your ideas and they land. The verse names the bind you are in, not a flaw in you.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You worked ten years and the promotion went to someone else, feeling unseen here. Bhartrihari cries out to his own hope, saying he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart while trying to please the wicked. Today, this speaks to the cost of waiting for recognition that never arrives. You might notice what you are still swallowing in that same hope, and what empty laughter still costs you.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks to his own hope after years of chasing money and approval. He tells it that he endured taunts from wicked people, held back his tears, and forced laughter with an empty heart. He folded his hands before those blinded by wealth. He asks how much longer this hope will make him dance in humiliation. After ten years of effort, the promotion went to another person, and you feel unseen at work. The verse names the price of waiting for recognition that keeps slipping away.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

reading: You feel that locals and westerners get the promotions while you do the work. Krishna says it is better to walk your own path, imperfectly, than to perform another's duty well. Your own effort, done honestly, carries no wrong, so the next step you take at your own desk can simply be yours.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield of after Arjuna has laid down his bow. Arjuna is torn between grief and duty. Krishna has just explained that perfection comes through worship offered in one's own work. Now he repeats that one's own duty, even if walked imperfectly, is better than another's duty performed perfectly. He adds that acting in line with one's own nature brings no fault, because every undertaking carries some flaw. You are doing the labor while others take the credit. The verse says your own effort, done honestly, carries no wrong. It does not erase the unfairness, but it places your work back in your own hands.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You are angry because your biggest client pays months late and treats you like a nobody in front of his staff. Bhartrihari cries out to hope, saying he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart, asking how much longer it will make him dance. Today, you might notice what you put up with because you still hope this client will value you; naming that pattern is a first step toward reclaiming your own standard.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks to his own hope from the Censure of Craving. He tells of enduring taunts from wicked people while trying to please them. He held back his tears and laughed with an empty heart. He folded his hands before those whose minds were numbed by money. He asks hope how much longer it will make him dance. You are angry because your biggest client pays months late and treats you like a nobody in front of his staff.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You dread Monday mornings because your director nitpicks your work while approving the same from others, and tells you to wait another cycle. Bhartrihari says that serving a master means any behaviour becomes a fault: stay quiet and you are dull, speak and you are a show-off, patient and you are weak. This verse names the impossible position you are in, not a flaw in you. Anchor in your own standard of the work itself, and let your submission stand on that measure alone.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this to the reader from his section on wicked people. He is describing the trap of anyone who serves a cruel master. No matter what the servant does, the master twists it into a fault. Stay silent and you are dull. Speak well and you are a show-off. Stay close and you are pushy. Keep away and you lack confidence. Be patient and you are weak. Refuse to tolerate it and you are ill bred. Serving another person is a deep duty. It is harder than the discipline of yogis. Your director turns every virtue into a fault. This verse names that trap for you, not a flaw in your work.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You feel angry because your TL took your name on the presentation in front of the client. Bhartrihari says that when you serve a powerful person, every choice is read as a fault: stay quiet and you are dull, speak and you are a show-off. The verse sees this double bind in the position itself, not in you. You can anchor in your own standard today, knowing that no reply you give will fully satisfy an unfair setup.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this from his section on the wicked. He addresses anyone who serves a master. The listener has just described how no behaviour escapes blame. The poet says that if you stay quiet you are dull, if you speak well you are a show-off, if you stay close you are pushy, if you keep away you lack confidence, if you are patient you are weak, and if you refuse to endure things you are ill-bred. He concludes that serving another person is a duty so deep that even yogis cannot master it. Your anger at the stolen credit is not a personal failing. It comes from serving someone who twists every response into a fault.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You feel hurt that your 20 years of experience from India counts for nothing here, and you report to someone half your age. Bhartrihari cries out to Hope: he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart, folding his hands before those numbed by money. Today, you too may be holding back tears and smiling through a role that asks you to perform for people who do not value your years. Notice the empty heart behind the forced laugh, and let your own hands rest from folding them.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to his own hope from the Censure of Craving. He has spent his life digging for treasure, flattering kings, and crossing seas for gain. Now he lists the humiliations he swallowed to win favour. He held back his tears and laughed with an empty heart. He folded his hands before people whose minds were numbed by money. He asks hope how much longer it will make him dance. You have carried twenty years of skill across a border only to find it treated as nothing, while you answer to someone younger. The verse names the cost of swallowing that slight to keep a place.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You feel overlooked again. Bhartrihari tells the reader that if you keep quiet you are dull, and if you speak you are a show-off; patient, you are weak; refuse to put up with things, you are ill-bred. Any behaviour can be read as a fault when you serve someone powerful, so the problem lies in the position, not in you. You can anchor in your own standard today, rather than searching for the one right behaviour that will finally earn you recognition.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this from his section on wicked people. He addresses anyone who serves a master. The verse lists a trap. If you stay silent, you are dull. If you speak well, you are a show-off. If you stay close, you are pushy. If you keep away, you lack confidence. If you are patient, you are weak. If you refuse to tolerate things, you are ill-bred. He concludes that serving another person is a duty so deep that even yogis cannot master it. You feel overlooked again. The verse shows that the trap is in the position, not in you.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: Your manager calls you quiet in your review after talking over you in every meeting. Bhartrihari says that serving a boss means any choice is read as a fault: stay silent and you are dull, speak up and you are a show-off. This double bind belongs to the power imbalance, not to you. You can anchor in your own standard of speaking up, trusting that your voice has worth even when it is dismissed.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his Niti Shatakam as a warning about serving a cruel master. He tells the reader that a wicked boss twists every virtue into a fault. Stay silent and you are dull. Speak well and you are a show-off. Stay close and you are pushy. Keep away and you lack confidence. Be patient and you are weak. Refuse to endure things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis who gain insight through contemplation. Your manager twists your silence into dullness after silencing you in every meeting. The bind belongs to the power imbalance, not to your worth.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: Ram says the news itself did not burn his heart; what hurt was that the king did not face him and tell him directly. You are feeling the sting of a co-founder taking all the credit alone in front of investors, as if your part never existed. The deepest pain here can be that the truth was not met face to face between you.
meaning: Ram speaks to Kaikeyi after he has accepted fourteen years of exile. He agrees to leave without anger. Yet one thing still burns. He tells her that the news itself is not his sorrow. What hurts is that his father did not come to him and tell him directly. He can accept the loss. He cannot accept being kept in the dark by the one he loves. Your co-founder took the credit alone in front of the investors. The loss of recognition is one thing. The deeper sting is that the truth was not met face to face between you.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: Ram says the loss itself was bearable, yet what burns his heart is that the king did not face him and tell him directly. When a parent’s words leave you feeling unseen, the wound can sit less in the event than in the silence around it. You might let that exact ache—being spoken around rather than to—be present with you today, without forcing it into any larger story.
meaning: Ram has just agreed to leave for the forest for fourteen years after Kaikeyi demands it. He accepts the exile without anger. Yet one thing still burns him. He tells Kaikeyi that the loss itself was bearable. What hurts is that his father did not come to him and tell him the news himself. Your parents chose to speak around you rather than to you. That gap between what happened and who faced you with it is the real weight you carry now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You feel lonely while raising your kids. Krishna tells Arjuna, 'See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.' This means no distance can break the bond of being truly seen. You might find a quiet moment today to notice one ordinary thing around you and let yourself be held by that.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just described the yogi who sees the self in all beings. Now he restates that unity in his own voice. He says that whoever sees him everywhere and sees everything resting within him is never separated from him, and he is never separated from that person. The verse proposes a steady moderation of attention, bringing the mind back again and again to one shared presence. You are raising your children in a home where your husband's family speaks of you behind your back and your husband offers no defense. That absence of being seen by the people closest to you is a real loneliness.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You carry the weight of words that called you a burden, and since that day something inside has felt broken. Krishna says that harsh words from relatives keep burning him, day after day, the way fire-sticks are churned. That same slow burn can meet you today, not as a mark against you, but as a truth Krishna himself named: that family words can linger and ache.
meaning: Krishna speaks these words to the sage Narada after he has grown weary of the feuds within his own clan. He tells Narada that he gives his relatives half of what he owns and bears their harsh words, yet those words still grind his heart like a fire-stick being churned to kindle flame. The verse proposes that in family quarrels the only effective weapon is not iron but softness, meaning generosity, patience, sincerity, gentleness and respect.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You gave up your career to care for your mother, yet your siblings tell everyone you are only doing it for the house. Ram says the one sorrow that burns his heart is not the news itself, but that the person he loved did not face him and tell him directly. Today, the sting may be that your own family speaks about your sacrifice behind your back rather than naming it to your face.
meaning: Ram speaks these words to Kaikeyi after he has accepted fourteen years in the forest. He agrees at once and shows no anger. Yet one thing still burns inside him. He tells Kaikeyi that the only sorrow is that his father did not come himself to tell him about Bharata's coronation. The verse proposes that a person can bear the loss itself. What wounds is the absence of a direct face to face telling from the one they love.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You have sent money home for 15 years, yet your brother claims you never did anything for the family. Krishna says his relatives' harsh words keep burning him day after day, churned like a fire-stick. That sting of being erased despite your giving can still burn now. Let that fire-stick rest; the verse simply names the heat your brother's words left behind.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing weary of feuds inside his own clan. He tells Narada that he gives his relatives half of all he owns and bears their harsh words, yet those words still churn his heart like someone grinding a fire-stick to spark a flame. The verse proposes that in family quarrels the only effective weapon is one not made of iron, namely generosity, patience, sincerity, gentleness and respect. You have sent money home for fifteen years, and now your brother says you did nothing for the family. The verse names the particular sting of being erased despite your giving.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after he has grown weary of feuds inside his own clan. His relatives are split into two factions, and they keep speaking harsh words to him. He tells Narada that their cruel speech grinds his heart like someone rubbing a fire-stick to make flame. The verse proposes that in family conflict, the only effective weapon is not iron but softness: generosity, patience, sincerity, gentleness and respect.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has lain on the shore for three days asking the ocean for a way across. No answer comes.
verse_text.line: Calm, patience, honesty and kind words: people who don't value them will read them as weakness.
verse_text.translation: See the ocean's arrogance: he does not even show himself. Calm, forbearance, straightforwardness and gentle speech, these virtues of the good, are taken by the unworthy as signs of weakness.

verse_text.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse_text.speaker: Prahlada (quoted by Draupadi)
verse_text.setting: Draupadi quotes old Prahlada answering his grandson: is forgiveness better, or force?
verse_text.line: Force isn't always right, and forgiveness isn't always right. Wisdom is knowing which the moment needs.
verse_text.translation: Force is not always best, and forgiveness is not always best. Know this for certain, my child: both have their place.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Uttanka, furious that the war happened, threatens to curse Krishna for not stopping it.
verse_text.line: I tried hard to make peace. When people refuse to be reconciled, you can't force it.
verse_text.translation: I made every effort earlier to bring the Kauravas to peace. But they could not be brought to agree, however I tried.

verse_text.speaker: Seer
verse_text.setting: The creation story: last of all, dharma is made.
verse_text.line: Nothing is higher than what is right. With it the weak can face the strong. What is right is truth.
verse_text.translation: Still he did not flourish. So he created a higher form, dharma. Dharma is the power over power; nothing is higher than dharma. Through dharma even a weak man can stand up to a strong one, as with the help of a king. That dharma is truth. So people say of one who speaks truth, 'He speaks dharma,' and of one who speaks dharma, 'He speaks truth.' Both are the same.

days.reading: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says that nothing is higher than what is right, and through it even the weak can face the strong. You could write down one truth about yourself today and place it where you will see it. That truth stands on its own, separate from the harsh words spoken to you.

verse_text.speaker: Kabandha
verse_text.setting: Ram is lost and grieving; Kabandha tells him to seek Sugriva, who has also lost his wife and home.
verse_text.line: Find a friend who knows your kind of trouble. You won't get through this alone.
verse_text.translation: You must make him your friend, best of friends. Thinking it over, I see no success for you without it.

days.reading: Kabandha tells Rama, who is lost and grieving, to make a best friend of someone who knows the same kind of trouble, because without that friendship success is not in sight. You could reach out to a classmate or peer who understands what it feels like when harsh words from home cut deep. Shared experience can make for help that actually works.

story.title: Hanuman finds a friend in Lanka
story.summary: Searching Lanka, Hanuman is surprised to find a house with Ram's name on it. Its owner, Vibhishan, Ravana's brother, says he lives in Lanka like a tongue among teeth. Hanuman tells him even a restless monkey like himself was given Ram's love.
story.lesson: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.

days.reading: In the Sundar Kand, Vibhishan tells Hanuman he lives in Lanka like a tongue among teeth, surrounded by people whose values he does not share. He admits he has no practice or love for Ram's feet, yet finding Hanuman brings him rest. This speaks to your hurt from harsh words at home, showing that even inside a place where you cannot be honest, one true connection can bring quiet rest.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: Krishna tells Narada that harsh words from relatives keep burning him day after day, churning his heart like a fire-stick. You are feeling this same sting in your own home, where criticism and dismissal from those closest to you leave a steady ache. The verse names that family words can burn long after they are spoken, without saying you caused the heat.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after weariness with feuds inside his own clan. He tells Narada that his heart is churned like a fire-stick by the harsh words his relatives speak. The verse proposes that in family conflict the only effective weapon is not iron but gentleness, patience and respect. Your mother-in-law criticises your raising of the children and your husband calls you too sensitive, so the words keep burning inside the home you share.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: You carry an ache from betrayal by those closest to you. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet no one else truly knows this private hurt; only the heart knows the love it misses. Today, naming this grief to even one safe person might ease its weight, while you hold the truth of what was lost within you.
meaning: In the Sundar Kand of the Ramcharitmanas, Hanuman has reached Sita in the grove and dropped Ram's ring before telling her Ram's whole story. Sita, captive and threatened by Ravana, has nearly lost hope. Ram's message through Hanuman says that speaking of pain lightens it a little, but there is no one to tell because no one else knows this ache. Only Ram's own heart knows the truth of the love between him and Sita. You carry an ache from betrayal by those closest to you. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet no one else truly knows this private hurt; only the heart knows the love it misses.

verse_text.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
verse_text.speaker: Ashma (quoted by Vyasa)
verse_text.setting: The sage Ashma answers King Janaka, who asks how to stay steady when people and wealth come and go.
verse_text.line: Mental pain comes from two places: something you didn't want happened, or your mind is spinning. No third.
verse_text.translation: Sorrow of the mind has only two sources: a confused, wandering mind, or something unwanted happening to you. There is no third.

days.reading: Ashma tells King Janaka that mental pain comes from only two places: something unwanted happened to you, or your mind is spinning in confusion. This verse sees your ache as arising from one of those two sources, not from any hidden fault within you. Notice whether your pain points to the betrayal itself, or to a mind that keeps circling it.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: Closing verse of the section on steadfastness.
verse_text.line: A cut tree grows back; the waning moon fills again. Remembering this, the wise do not despair.
verse_text.translation: A tree that is cut grows again; the waning moon waxes again in the world. Reflecting on this, the good are not tormented in this world.

days.reading: Bhartrihari writes that a cut tree grows back and the waning moon fills again. You carry the ache of betrayal by your own family, yet this verse points to how loss in nature is followed by regrowth. Let the image of the moon returning to fullness give you ground to stand on today.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha on the fourth gatekeeper: good company (satsanga).
verse_text.line: Even at your lowest and most helpless, don't let go of good company.
verse_text.translation: Even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little.

days.reading: Vasishtha tells Rama that even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little. This speaks to your feeling of being lost after betrayal by your own family. You can hold one thread to someone who steadies you, even for a few minutes, without dropping anyone or forcing yourself to perform.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Wherever the restless mind wanders, gently bring it back. Again and again.
verse_text.translation: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, from there one should draw it back and bring it under the control of the self.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to draw his restless mind back again and again, wherever it wanders. Your mind may keep returning to the family who betrayed you. You could try noticing where it has gone, then gently guiding it back to one steady breath or sound today.

verse_text.speaker: Narada
verse_text.setting: Narada gives Shuka a plain remedy for pain that cannot be fixed.
verse_text.line: Not dwelling on it is the medicine. Brooding doesn't make pain leave; it makes it grow.
verse_text.translation: When pain of body or mind arrives and nothing can be done about it, do not keep thinking about it. Not dwelling on it is the medicine for sorrow; brooding does not make it leave, it only makes it grow.

days.reading: Narada tells Shuka that when pain arrives and nothing can fix it, do not keep dwelling on it. Brooding does not make sorrow leave; it only makes it grow. You could try setting a small timer for five minutes to feel the ache, then gently shift your attention to one task in front of you.

story.title: Nala and Damayanti
story.summary: King Nala, possessed by the spirit Kali, gambles away his kingdom to his brother and abandons Damayanti in the forest. Years of separation and disguise follow, until Nala masters the dice and the two are reunited.
story.lesson: Compulsions can take everything. Loyalty and patience can still bring you home.

days.reading: Damayanti wakes alone in a forest full of lions, in half a garment, and walks for days until she reaches Chedi dusty and thin. There, a queen mother takes her in, and Damayanti agrees to serve as a maid while setting her own conditions: she will not eat leftovers, will not wash feet, and will not speak with other men. Even in total loss, she grieves openly and still decides the terms on which she will live, naming what she will and will not accept.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You trusted a friend with your business and were stabbed in the back. Bhartrihari cries out to Hope, saying he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart while trying to please the wicked. Today, that same hollow performance may still feel heavy, yet the verse simply names the cost of swallowing taunts to keep hoping. Let the empty laughter remind you where your trust was misplaced, and let that clarity shape the next boundary you keep.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to his own Hope from the Censure of Craving. He lists the humiliations he endured while chasing money and approval. He swallowed insults, held back tears, and forced laughter before people numbed by wealth. He asks how much longer Hope will make him dance in this empty performance. The verse proposes that unexamined hope for gain or approval consumes our lives while we pretend to be content. You opened your work to a friend and they betrayed you. Bhartrihari names the same hollow cost you may still carry after that trust broke.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: You have carried this silence for two years since your daughter stopped speaking to you after a disagreement about her marriage. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet no one else can know the full ache, and only the heart alone knows the love it misses. Today, the truth of what you miss may live quietly inside you, known fully by your own heart.
meaning: Ram sends this message to Sita through Hanuman while she is held captive. Sita has nearly lost hope after long separation from Ram. Ram says that speaking of pain lightens it a little, but there is no one who can fully know this ache. Only Ram's own heart knows the truth of the love between them. The message offers that being remembered can carry someone through near despair. Your daughter's silence has left a grief that no one around you can fully map, yet your own heart knows exactly what you miss.

verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: 'My Plan of Campaign', Madras, February 1897, on friends who turned critics.
verse_text.line: as soon as he dares to differ, that sympathy is gone, that love vanishes.
verse_text.translation: We hear so much tall talk in this world, of liberal ideas and sympathy with differences of opinion. That is very good, but as a fact, we find that one sympathises with another only so long as the other believes in everything he has to say, but as soon as he dares to differ, that sympathy is gone, that love vanishes.

reading: You feel hurt because the warmth you expected from your parents vanished when you spoke up. Swami Vivekananda observed that sympathy often lasts only while the other person agrees with everything said, and vanishes as soon as someone dares to differ. Today, this can show you that their reaction points to conditions they placed on their support, not to any wrong in your voice.
meaning: Swami Vivekananda spoke these words to an audience at Victoria Hall in Madras during February eighteen ninety seven. He had just returned from America and was facing critics who claimed others had made his success there. He told his listeners that people often praise liberal ideas and sympathy. Yet in practice, a person offers sympathy only while the other agrees with everything. The moment someone dares to differ, that sympathy disappears and the love vanishes. Your parents acted as if your hurt was drama only after you voiced a difference. The verse shows their warmth depended on agreement, not on your wellbeing.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You carry the sting of harsh words spoken by your own brother at a wedding, with everyone laughing along. Krishna says his heart is churned like a fire-stick, burned day after day by the harsh words his relatives say. That same slow burn can be yours today, naming the exact wound without forcing it to heal faster than it will.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing tired of feuds within his own clan. He tells Narada that he gives his relatives half of what he owns, yet their harsh words still grind his heart like a fire-stick being churned for flame. The verse proposes that in family conflict the only effective weapon is not iron but softness: patience, generosity, sincerity and respect. Your brother's words at the wedding still turn in you like that fire-stick, long after the music stopped.

Your own heart alone knows the love you miss right now, and naming that loneliness is already a small relief.

Hanuman has just dropped Ram's ring from a tree and told her Ram's whole story. Ram says that telling grief lightens it a little, but asks whom he can tell, because no one else knows this pain. Only Ram's own heart knows the truth of the love between them. Your own heart alone knows the love you miss right now, and naming that loneliness is already a small relief.

verse_text.speaker: the gopis
verse_text.setting: The women of Braj, after Krishna has left, on missing him.
verse_text.line: "Since he left, it has been monsoon in our eyes."
verse_text.translation: Night and day our eyes keep raining. Ever since Shyam went away, it is always the rainy season for us.

reading: You feel empty as the house echoes on weekends. The gopis say that ever since he left, it has been monsoon in their eyes, night and day. Your missing him can feel like weather that does not lift, and naming that plainly is part of how you still hold what you love. Let those tears be the rain the verse speaks of.
meaning: The gopis speak to a friend after Krishna has left Braj. They tell her that since Shyam went away, their eyes rain night and day without stopping. They say the rainy season has settled over their sight. The verse proposes that tears for someone you miss are allowed. The loss is so total that weeping becomes a season rather than a single event. Your husband has left and the house echoes on weekends. The gopis name a grief that does not lift, and your missing him can feel like weather that simply stays.

meaning: The gopis speak to a friend after Krishna leaves Braj. They tell her that since Shyam went away, their eyes keep raining night and day. The rainy season has become their state. verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You have shared a bed for nine years without truly meeting. Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever sees him everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him, and he is never lost to them. In your quiet distance, this can mean that a bond deeper than shared walls still holds you, even when the worlds between you feel vast.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after describing the yogi who sees the self in all beings. He restates the vision in his own voice. He says that one who sees him everywhere and sees everything resting in him is never out of his sight, and he is never out of theirs. The verse proposes a gentle, repeated return of attention. It asks the mind to settle by noticing one presence inside all that appears. You have shared a bed for nine years without truly meeting. Even in that quiet distance, a bond deeper than shared walls still holds you, though the worlds between you feel vast.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You are searching the last few years for the moment love slipped away, yet the mind keeps replaying what it cannot find. Krishna hears Arjuna say the mind is restless, stormy and as hard to hold as the wind. Your thoughts circling the sale of the house are that same wind; you do not have to catch them. Let the search rest for now, and notice one breath that is not searching.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He has heard about a steady mind, and he objects. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He thinks it is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse names this difficulty honestly. It says the mind is hard to steady, but practice and letting go can train it. You are trying to find the exact moment your partner's love slipped away, yet the mind keeps replaying what it cannot locate.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: Ram says the one sorrow burning his heart is that the king did not tell him himself about Bharata's coronation. You carry the weight of a bond ending with a sudden block after years. The verse names that the wound can sit in how the news reached you, not only in the loss itself. You might let that precise sting sit with you today, as Ram let his sorrow remain without rushing past it.
meaning: Rama speaks to Kaikeyi after he has accepted fourteen years of exile. He agrees at once and shows no anger. Yet one thing still burns inside him. He says only this sorrow remains. His father did not tell him the news himself. The verse points to a hard truth. You cannot control what happens to you. You can control the person who walks out of the room without facing you. You are carrying a bond that ended with a sudden block after three years. The verse names that the wound can sit in how the news reached you, not only in the loss itself.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You are 8000 miles away while your mother lives alone in Indore. Krishna tells his mother Yashoda that since leaving her, no one has called him by his pet name, and he has missed his morning breakfast and evening warm milk. This shows that even far from home, the ache for ordinary tenderness—being known by a home name and being fed—is real. Your distance does not erase that longing; it simply names what you miss today.
meaning: Krishna sends a message through to his foster mother Yashoda while he is in Mathura. He tells her to stay well and that they will visit in a few days. He also tells her that since the day he left her, no one has called him by his pet name Kanhaiya. He has not had his morning breakfast or his evening warm milk. The verse shows that missing home is love. Even as a prince, he longs for the ordinary tenderness of being known by a home name and being fed. Your distance from Indore does not cancel the ache for being called by your home name and being cared for. It simply names what is missing right now.

It is the love that makes the distance hard.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: Arjuna asks this, and many of us ask it too: what pushes a person to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? If you're carrying something you did, you've probably asked it at night. The Gita treats the question as worth a full answer.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their will, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this desire is the enemy that clouds wisdom. Seeing this clearly is the first step toward mastering it. You feel you did something wrong before your parents left, and now their aging faces sit with you. The verse names the pull behind actions you did not want to take, without calling you wicked.

This speaks to your restlessness today: the ache is not only in your travelling limits, but in missing the ordinary tenderness of home, and the message home that you are holding on and will come soon carries that same quiet love.
meaning: Krishna sends a message through to his foster mother Yashoda. He is far away in Mathura after killing. He tells her to stay well and that the brothers will visit in four or five days. He also says that since he left her, no one has called him by his pet name Kanhaiya. He has not eaten morning breakfast or drunk warm milk in the evening. The verse proposes that missing home is love. It shows that the one who is away also longs for the small tenderness of being known at home. Your restlessness carries the same two-way ache. You miss the ordinary tenderness of home while you stay put at sixty-four.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Arjuna says this, and he was the finest archer of his time. He admits his own mind won't obey him. If yours keeps replaying the same conversation at 2 a.m., you are in good company, and the Gita takes the problem seriously before it offers anything.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the field. He has just heard about the steady evenness of a perfected yogi. He objects that such calm cannot last. The mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse records this honest complaint and sets up the need for practice and letting go to train it.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel anxious while raising your kids. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and that these come and go without lasting. You can notice this anxiety as something that arrives and departs, without letting it sweep you into panic or despair. Rest in the simple fact that this feeling, like the weather, has its own beginning and end.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These states arrive and depart on their own. They do not last. Arjuna must bear them with patience. Your anxiety rises and falls like the weather Krishna describes. It is not the whole of who you are, and it will not stay forever.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: Between school runs, swim class, homework, and work calls, your days feel squeezed with no room to breathe as a dad. The Yoga Vasishtha describes a mind caught on endless waves of tasks, fainting in a net of reckonings: 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do.' That same loop may be running in the background of your life today. You might notice one small moment—perhaps the pause after a work call—where the mind stops its tally and simply rests.
meaning: Two old friends meet again after many years apart. Bhasa admits to Vilasa that he has never found peace. Bhasa explains that a person is carried along by endless waves of tasks. The mind never rests because it keeps tallying what is done, what is being done, and what must still be done. Without inner understanding, years of hard effort leave a person exactly where they started. Your days of school runs, swim class, homework and work calls carry the same tallying mind. The verse names the loop you are already in, without calling it a failure on your part.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Your daughter is two and a half and still does not speak, and each night the same thought returns. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. When your thoughts loop at night, this verse names that struggle as real rather than a failure. Rest beside your sleeping daughter, feeling the stillness of her breath, and let the wind of the mind move without forcing it to stop.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after hearing about the steady evenness of the highest yogi. He confesses that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and he finds it as hard to hold as the wind. The verse takes this complaint seriously and names the difficulty of mastering the mind. Your nightly loop about your daughter's silence is not a failure of care. It is the mind doing what Arjuna describes, and it can be named without shame.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: When the mind chases a wandering sense, it is swept off like a boat in the wind.
verse_text.translation: When the mind runs after the roving senses, it carries away one's understanding, as the wind carries a boat away on the water.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that when the mind chases a wandering sense, it is swept off like a boat in the wind. Your overthinking can begin with one small detail that pulls your attention, and then the mind follows it farther out. You can notice when your mind has just followed that thought, and gently bring your attention back to the present moment with your daughter.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Like a lamp in a windless place that doesn't flicker: that's a settled mind.
verse_text.translation: As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker: that is the image used for the yogi of controlled mind practising union with the self.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that a mind at rest is like a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker. Your mind keeps moving even when you wish it would stop. You can let it settle for a few minutes at a time, sheltered from the winds around it, while the flame still gives light.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Little by little, with patience and steady resolve, settle the mind and let other thoughts go.
verse_text.translation: Little by little one should come to rest, with understanding held steady; fixing the mind on the self, one should think of nothing else.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to settle the mind little by little, with patience and steady resolve, letting other thoughts go. This gradual calming speaks to a mind that replays the day and lies awake looping. You can rest your attention on one steady point right now, without forcing the noise to vanish all at once.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Yes, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But practice and letting go can train it.
verse_text.translation: The Blessed Lord said: Undoubtedly, mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and hard to control. But it is held by practice and by detachment, Kaunteya.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the mind is indeed restless and hard to hold, yet it can be trained by steady practice and by loosening its grip on what it chases. You could try gently returning your attention to your daughter’s presence for a few breaths, then loosening your grip on the thought that loops each night. This is not about forcing silence, but about repeating a small return.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Wherever the restless mind wanders, gently bring it back. Again and again.
verse_text.translation: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, from there one should draw it back and bring it under the control of the self.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to draw the restless mind back wherever it wanders, again and again. Your mind is doing exactly what Krishna describes: wandering, then returning. Today, when a thought loops, you could simply notice where it has gone and gently bring your attention back to your daughter’s face.

story.title: Pingala's song
story.summary: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira about Pingala, who sat awake one night waiting for a lover who never came. Every sound outside might have been his footsteps, so she kept listening. Late in the night she saw what was keeping her awake. It was her hope that someone else would arrive and settle her. She let that hope go, and she slept peacefully.
story.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.

days.reading: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira about Pingala, who sat awake waiting for a lover who never came. She kept listening for every sound, until she saw that her hope of someone else arriving was what kept her awake. Letting go of that expectation let her sleep peacefully. Your mind keeps listening through the night, hoping an answer will arrive to settle it, yet releasing that waiting can bring the rest you are looking for.

reading: Your mind feels as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna hears Arjuna say this: the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, and holding it feels impossible. You do not have to steady it by force today. Notice one breath, then let the next one come, just as the wind moves on its own.

verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what becomes of someone who tries and fails; Krishna reassures him.
verse_text.line: What happens to someone who believes, tries, slips, and doesn't make it to the end?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: One who has faith but does not strive enough, whose mind falls away from yoga before reaching perfection, what end does he come to, Krishna?

reading: You have been telling yourself you will start the gym on Monday since January. In the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna asks Krishna what happens to someone who believes, tries, slips, and does not reach the end. This question speaks to you today because your repeated starts feel like failures; yet Arjuna is only asking, not declaring ruin. Your January intention remains a real step you took, not an empty one.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna what becomes of a person who begins with faith but whose effort is not strong enough, and whose mind falls away from yoga before reaching perfection. Krishna answers that no sincere effort is wasted, because the person picks up again exactly where they left off. Your repeated intention to start the gym is not a string of failures. It is real effort that carries forward, even when the body has not yet shown results.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.

reading: You have opened your essay document fifteen times and written only the title. Rama tells the sages that the mind swoops onto a task like a bird onto food, then drops it like a bored child's toy. Let the title sit there, and notice the bird simply landing and leaving, without judging the landing.
meaning: Rama speaks to the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha after they ask why he has grown so withdrawn. He describes what he has seen of the world and of his own mind. You are facing an essay due on Friday and the blank page feels like a wall. Rama names this gap between starting and dropping as ordinary motion, not a flaw in you.

verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.

verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You have wanted to write a book for ten years, yet not one chapter is finished. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or pleasures mean to him, and who he really is. When everything you do feels hollow, this question can be the start of finding what matters to you today.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: Arjuna asks this, and many of us ask it too: what pushes a person to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? If you're carrying something you did, you've probably asked it at night. The Gita treats the question as worth a full answer.

The verse names the pull behind that stillness, not as a flaw in you, but as a force that can be seen.
