verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people turn to the divine: the distressed, the seeker of wealth, the seeker of knowledge, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among them. The verse simply names this path as welcome, without asking what comes after.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded and the wrongdoers do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. These are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four kinds worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Your curiosity is one of the doors Krishna names. It places you among those who turn toward the search without needing another reason first.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel anxious right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go through sense-contact, and do not last. You can bear this discomfort as something that begins and ends, without letting it sweep you into panic or despair.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna grieves the coming loss of kin. Krishna reminds him that the Self inside never dies and never is born. Yet the body meets cold and heat, pleasure and pain through the senses. These touchings begin and end on their own. They do not last. A person must bear them without giving in to joy or grief. The anxiety you carry now is a passing touch, not the whole of who you are. It begins and ends without defining the life you are still living.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Without inner discipline there's no clarity; without clarity, no peace; and without peace, where is happiness?
verse_text.translation: For the undisciplined there is no understanding and no steady contemplation. Without contemplation there is no peace, and for the one without peace, where is happiness?

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that without inner discipline there is no clarity, and without clarity no peace, so where is happiness? The verse sees stress stealing happiness through a chain: an unsettled mind loses its collected focus, which breaks contemplation and peace. Amid the rush of tatkal ticket booking timing, this points to how chasing quick relief keeps the mind from standing still, rather than naming any fault in you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on working in the world without being stained by it.
verse_text.line: Like a lotus leaf in water, do your work without letting the mess soak in.
verse_text.translation: One who acts offering all actions to the Supreme, giving up attachment, is not touched by wrong, as a lotus leaf is not wet by water.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever acts while offering the action up and letting go of attachment stays unstained, as a lotus leaf sits in water without getting wet. Amid the rush to catch tatkal ticket windows and the pressure closing in from every side, you can do your work fully while letting the surrounding mess roll off. Let the surface stay dry even while you remain in the pond.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Rivers pour into the ocean and it stays full and still. Let desires enter you the same way.
verse_text.translation: As waters enter the ocean, which is ever being filled yet stays unmoved within its shores, so the one into whom all desires enter in the same way finds peace, not the one who craves desires.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that rivers pour into the ocean yet it stays full and still. Let desires enter you the same way. With the timing of your ticket booking always pressing, demands will keep flowing in. Peace is found in being deep enough to take them in without being moved, not in craving calm that depends on circumstances.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Moderate in food and rest, in work and play, in sleep and waking: that's how sorrow eases.
verse_text.translation: For one who is moderate in food and recreation, measured in effort at work, moderate in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that yoga destroys sorrow when one is moderate in food, recreation, work, sleep and waking. You could try setting one fixed boundary today, such as stopping work at a set hour or taking a short break before your next booking rush. This measured rhythm supports the steadiness you are building through the week.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse_text.line: Hand your work to something higher, drop the 'mine' and the hoping, and act with the fever gone.
verse_text.translation: Surrendering all actions to me, with your mind on the inner self, free from hope and the sense of 'mine', fight with your fever gone.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to hand his work to the Lord, drop the sense of 'mine' and anxious hoping, and act with the fever gone. You could try offering today's tasks to something larger than your worry before you begin, then do them without gripping the outcome. The work still gets done, but the heat inside drops.

story.title: Janaka on the palace roof
story.summary: Walking in his garden one spring, King Janaka overheard hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbed to his palace roof and questioned everything he had lived for. When his attendant came to call him to the day's work, he could have walked away from the throne. He didn't. He went back and did his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutched.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

days.reading: King Janaka heard hidden sages sing of the self, climbed to his palace roof, and questioned everything, yet when his attendant called him to work, he stayed and did his duties without clutching. You face the pressure of tatkal ticket booking timing, where demands close in from all sides. You can carry the same steady mind into that rush, doing the task without letting it grip you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that people turn toward the divine through distress, curiosity, need, or wisdom, and all four are counted among the good. Your curiosity right now places you in that company. You do not have to wait until you have answers to belong here.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. It does not ask for a pure motive first. Your curiosity right now places you in that company. You do not have to wait until you have answers to belong here.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You carry a hopeful feeling right now. Lakshmana tells Ram that there is no strength greater than enthusiasm, and for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. That energy of will can meet what lies ahead of you today, turning a small step of resolve into forward motion.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Ram is overwhelmed by longing for Sita. Every bird and mated deer reminds him of her, and his grief deepens. Lakshman pulls him out of despair and tells him that enthusiasm is powerful. There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. The verse proposes that resolute energy is the root of all effort, and by it alone the brothers will recover Sita. You carry a hopeful feeling right now. That same energy of will can meet what lies ahead of you today, turning a small step of resolve into forward motion.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You feel lost right now. Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra that Arjuna set down his bow and sank onto his chariot seat, his mind overwhelmed by grief. This verse names the moment when everything feels too heavy to carry on. It points to the very place where Arjuna stopped, not as a final failure, but as the place where help arrives next.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just argued that killing his own kin would destroy their families and ways of life. He says he would rather be killed unarmed. Overcome by grief and fear, Arjuna puts down his bow and arrows and sinks onto the seat of his chariot, too overwhelmed to go on. You are between things right now, and this verse names the exact moment when the weight of everything becomes too much to carry forward.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You feel peaceful right now. Krishna says the one whose happiness, delight and light are all within becomes one with Brahman and reaches lasting peace. That inner gladness can stay steady even when work shifts around you, pointing toward a freedom that does not depend on what happens outside.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He describes the wise person who has seen clearly. This person keeps happiness, delight and light inside themselves. They do not depend on things that begin and end. Such a yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman while still living. That inner steadiness can sit beside your work without vanishing when shifts change around you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that people turn toward the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom, and all four are welcome. Your curiosity places you among those who seek, and that alone counts as a genuine opening. You can simply sit with this question today, letting it be what it is.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just explained that those who act from delusion do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of people who do. These are the distressed, the curious, those who need something, and the wise. He says all four worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Your curiosity places you among those who seek, and that alone counts as a genuine opening.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You feel restless while studying. Bali says, 'Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.' That sense of being stuck in the same loop can open a genuine question about what your days are actually for. You might notice one small shift in how you approach today's work, letting the repetition itself point toward something you still want to understand.
meaning: The demon king Bali has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day he sits by his window and notices that his days repeat in the same chain of tasks. He speaks these words to himself. He feels that the endless cycle of day and night mocks a thinking person. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the work is not to add more of it but to master the mind that runs it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one the world follows. As you move through success while raising your kids, your everyday choices quietly shape what they learn to value. Let your actions reflect the steadiness you hope to see around you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has asked why he must fight when he feels the weight of killing his own kin. Krishna answers that even those who have found complete fulfillment do not simply rest. They continue to act for the good of the world. The verse states that whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows. It proposes that people copy real conduct, not spoken words. A fulfilled person keeps showing up because their example keeps the world steady. You are moving through a season of success while raising your children. Your daily choices quietly teach them what matters more than any lecture you give.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that people turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom, and all four are welcome. You are standing in curiosity right now, and that doorway is counted among the good. Let this verse meet you exactly where you are, without asking you to become anything other than what you already are.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded and the wrongdoers do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four kinds worship him. In plain modern words, whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Distress, curiosity, need, or wisdom, each opens a valid door. You are standing in curiosity right now, and that doorway is counted among the good. Let this verse meet you exactly where you are, without asking you to become anything other than what you already are.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

days.reading: Arjuna tells Krishna that his nature is stricken by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right, so he asks to be taught plainly what is best. You are curious about the Gita itself, and here a student admits his own judgement has failed and asks for a clear answer. You can set aside the search for a cheap hotel in Rishikesh for a moment and simply sit with the question of what is best, ready to learn.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and these simply come and go without lasting. Like the search for hotels in Rishikesh under 3000 a night, some conditions are temporary and shift on their own. You can stand with the fact that this discomfort, too, has a beginning and an end, bearing it without panic.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna, 'Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.' For you, this means giving your full attention to the effort and craft you can control, while letting the outcome be what it will be. It offers ground to stand on: fear of the result is not a reason to stop showing up.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna, 'Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. The self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.' Since you are curious about how the Gita speaks to ordinary life, you could notice the next time you search for a quiet place like a Rishikesh hotel, and offer yourself the same patience you would show a friend finding their footing.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: Learn from those who have seen the truth: approach with humility, ask real questions, and serve.
verse_text.translation: Learn it by bowing down, by questioning, and by service. Those who are wise and have seen the truth will teach you that knowledge.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to learn from those who have seen the truth by bowing down, asking questions, and serving. Since you are curious about the Gita itself, you could seek one trustworthy commentary or study circle today and bring a genuine question you have about it. Approach it with humility, letting the teaching unfold through real inquiry rather than passive reading.

story.title: Action with devotion: surrender
story.summary: Krishna urges Arjuna to offer all action, warns that ego will only trip him, tells him to reflect fully and then choose, and finally to take refuge in him alone and not grieve.
story.lesson: Reflect fully, choose freely, and set down the fear.

days.reading: The teacher tells Arjuna he has shared the most secret knowledge and invites him to reflect fully, then choose as he wishes. Because Arjuna is dear to him, the teacher adds a final word: come to me alone for refuge and do not grieve. Your curiosity about where to stay in Rishikesh mirrors this openness to receive guidance before deciding your own path.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that people turn toward the divine through distress, curiosity, need, or wisdom, and all four kinds are welcome. Your curiosity is already one of those open doors. Let it carry you forward into this week's reading, simply noticing what the text says as you go.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. He says the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise all worship him. He means that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Your curiosity is already one of those open doors. It belongs here without needing to prove itself first.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people turn to the divine: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those in need, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among those welcomed with open regard. As you begin this week with the Gita, let this truth sit beside you: you are already counted among the good.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four worship him. In plain modern words, whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Your curiosity is one of those doors. It places you among those counted as good, without any proof of prior merit needed.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people turn to the divine: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those in need, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among these welcome seekers. The verse simply names your openness as a valid path toward what you are exploring.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after noting that deluded people do not turn to him. He names four kinds of good people who do worship him. These are the distressed, those who seek knowledge, those who seek wealth, and the wise. He says all four are welcome. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is valid. It does not demand a pure motive or a settled mind at the door. Your curiosity is already a door. It places you among those who turn toward something larger without needing to fix a wound first.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: My heart feels heavy as stone, but I don't cry, because of what people would think.
verse_text.translation: Though my heart is packed tight with the stones of life's sorrows, I don't let my tears fall, only out of fear of what my own people would think.

reading: It sounds like you're carrying something very heavy right now.

verse_text.speaker: Angiras
verse_text.setting: The two birds, continued.
verse_text.line: The bird that eats grieves, lost in its helplessness. When it sees the calm one beside it, grief falls away.
verse_text.translation: On the same tree a person sits sunk, grieving, bewildered by his own helplessness. When he sees the other, the content lord, and his greatness, his sorrow leaves him.

verse_text.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, CIII, p. 160
verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: Letter from Belur, 18 May 1901, ill and grieving the sudden death of the Raja of Khetri.
verse_text.line: Yet I am sure to bob up soon and am waiting for the next turn.
verse_text.translation: The Raja of Khetri died from a fall a few months ago. So you see things are all gloomy with me just now, and my own health is wretched. Yet I am sure to bob up soon and am waiting for the next turn.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: Closing verse of the section on steadfastness.
verse_text.line: A cut tree grows back; the waning moon fills again. Remembering this, the wise do not despair.
verse_text.translation: A tree that is cut grows again; the waning moon waxes again in the world. Reflecting on this, the good are not tormented in this world.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha on the fourth gatekeeper: good company (satsanga).
verse_text.line: Even at your lowest and most helpless, don't let go of good company.
verse_text.translation: Even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little.

verse_text.speaker: Kabandha
verse_text.setting: Ram is lost and grieving; Kabandha tells him to seek Sugriva, who has also lost his wife and home.
verse_text.line: Find a friend who knows your kind of trouble. You won't get through this alone.
verse_text.translation: You must make him your friend, best of friends. Thinking it over, I see no success for you without it.

story.title: Kabandha: find a friend who understands
story.summary: Freed from a curse, the creature Kabandha tells the grieving brothers to seek out Sugriva, an exile who has also lost his wife and home. Only a friend in the same trouble, he says, can help them now.
story.lesson: When you are lost, look for someone who has been through the same thing.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: My heart feels heavy as stone, but I don't cry, because of what people would think.
verse_text.translation: Though my heart is packed tight with the stones of life's sorrows, I don't let my tears fall, only out of fear of what my own people would think.

reading: It sounds like you're carrying something very heavy right now.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You have a plan and a date in mind. Bali says again day, again night, the same chain of tasks, and to a thinking person this feels like a mockery. That sense of repetition can meet your own empty feeling today, not as proof that your work is worthless, but as a prompt to ask what your days are actually for.
meaning: Bali speaks this to himself while sitting by his window after ruling the three worlds for ages. He notices that day follows night and the same tasks return without change. He tells himself that to a thinking person this endless loop feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the way forward is not more work but mastering the mind that runs it. You have a plan and a date in mind. That forward motion can sit beside this empty feeling today, as a prompt to ask what your days are actually for.

verse_text.speaker: Vibhishan
verse_text.setting: Vibhishan, Ravana's good-hearted brother, describes his life in Ravana's court.
verse_text.line: I live here like the tongue among the teeth.
verse_text.translation: Son of the wind, hear how I live: like the poor tongue among the teeth. Friend, knowing me to be without support, will the Lord of the Sun dynasty ever show me grace?

reading: It sounds like home doesn't feel safe right now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You feel hurt when your wife throws things in anger, and shame keeps you silent. Krishna says his own relatives' harsh words keep burning him day after day. The verse names that particular sting of being wounded by family, and how the hurt lingers. Today, your silence mirrors that same fire-stick churning—a real ache that does not vanish on its own.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing weary of feuds within his own clan. He tells Narada that his relatives speak harsh words which grind his heart like a fire-stick being churned for flame. The verse proposes that cruel speech from kin keeps burning a person long after it is spoken, and that the only effective weapon against such family trouble is gentleness, patience and respect rather than force. Your wife's anger lands as a wound from someone close, and the shame around it keeps the hurt alive inside you.

verse_text.speaker: Vidura
verse_text.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
verse_text.line: If you fear someone's anger or must tiptoe around them, they are not really your friend.
verse_text.translation: That is no friend whose anger you fear, or whom you must approach warily. A friend is one you can trust as you trust a father; the rest are mere acquaintances.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram, having embraced Vibhishan, asks how he survived in Lanka.
verse_text.line: You lived among the cruel day and night. I know how you kept your goodness.
verse_text.translation: 'You lived day and night among the wicked; how did you keep your goodness, friend? I know all your ways: very wise in conduct, with no taste for wrong.'

verse_text.speaker: Seer
verse_text.setting: The creation story: last of all, dharma is made.
verse_text.line: Nothing is higher than what is right. With it the weak can face the strong. What is right is truth.
verse_text.translation: Still he did not flourish. So he created a higher form, dharma. Dharma is the power over power; nothing is higher than dharma. Through dharma even a weak man can stand up to a strong one, as with the help of a king. That dharma is truth. So people say of one who speaks truth, 'He speaks dharma,' and of one who speaks dharma, 'He speaks truth.' Both are the same.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked.
verse_text.line: Avoid a cruel person even if brilliant. A snake wearing a jewel still bites.
verse_text.translation: A wicked person should be avoided, even if adorned with learning. Is a snake any less frightening because it wears a jewel?

verse_text.translation: You must make him your friend, best of friends. Thinking it over, I see no success for you without it.

story.title: Shunahshepa, the son neither parent chose to keep
story.summary: A king needs a human substitute for a lost sacrifice and offers a fortune for a son. The father says: I will never sell my eldest. The mother says: the youngest is my darling, I cannot part with him. The middle boy hears both sentences and understands his place in the house. He says it himself: then the middle one is sold. Take me.
story.lesson: When those who should protect you do not, you may seek refuge elsewhere and ask plainly for what you need.
